Newborn Cotton mice emerge into the world at a remarkably modest size, with a neonatal body mass of just 2 grams [Wwb = 2 grams]. This altricial state places them among the smallest rodents relative to adult size, and they depend entirely on maternal care during the critical first weeks of life. Under thermoneutral conditions, typically near 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C], the period of milk dependency lasts approximately 22 days after birth [tx = approximately 22 days after birth]. This relatively brief weaning phase is consistent with the rapid developmental trajectory observed in many small peromyscine rodents. The mother's energetic investment is considerable, as she must sustain lactation while simultaneously recovering from gestation. Following weaning, the young must quickly learn to forage independently, consuming seeds, insects, and fungi characteristic of the southeastern bottomland hardwood forests they inhabit. The onset of nutritional autonomy at this early age allows females to allocate resources toward subsequent litters within the same breeding season, a pattern essential for maintaining population densities in seasonally fluctuating environments.

Females of Peromyscus gossypinus typically experience a gestation lasting 22.8 days [tg = 22.8 days] when maintained at a core body temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C]. This duration is characteristic of the genus and reflects the efficient placental nourishment of a small litter. The timing of parturition is tightly linked to environmental conditions, with breeding activity peaking in spring and fall when moisture and food availability are highest. Reproductive output per event ranges from 1 to 7 pups per litter [N_R_i = 1 to 7 pups per litter], with the modal litter size centering on four or five offspring. Females can produce approximately 3 litters annually [F_R_i = approximately 3 litters annually], a frequency that varies with resource abundance and population density. This combination of moderate litter size and multiple annual reproductive events allows the species to recover quickly from population declines. The high intrinsic rate of increase is a key adaptation to life in frequently disturbed floodplain habitats, where predation pressure and periodic flooding impose significant mortality on all age classes.

The adult body mass of fully grown individuals reaches a maximum of 46 grams [Wwi = 46 grams], placing P. gossypinus as a medium-sized member of its genus. This ultimate wet weight is attained after a period of sustained growth following weaning, with males often achieving slightly larger sizes than females. The species' relatively robust physique is well suited to climbing and navigating the dense understory vegetation of its preferred habitats. In comparison to the old-field mouse, Peromyscus polionotus, which rarely exceeds 15 grams, the cotton mouse demonstrates a substantially larger body plan that may confer advantages in thermoregulation and competitive interactions. The energetic demands of maintaining this body mass are met through an opportunistic diet that shifts seasonally, incorporating arthropods, fleshy fruits, and mast when available. This dietary flexibility is critical for sustaining reproduction and survival throughout the year.

Puberty in female cotton mice is reached at an average of 58 days after birth [tp = 58 days after birth] under standard physiological temperatures of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C], though individual variation is considerable, with a documented range of 43 to 73 days after birth (43-73 days after birth) [tp = 43-73 days after birth]. This relatively early onset of sexual maturity is characteristic of many Peromyscus species inhabiting temperate and subtropical regions where extended breeding seasons reward rapid maturation. Males typically undergo testicular descent and spermatogenesis within a similar timeframe, ensuring synchronous reproductive readiness within populations. The variability in pubertal timing likely reflects both genetic factors and environmental influences, particularly the quality of maternal nutrition during the pre-weaning period. Early maturing females can contribute to the first cohort of the breeding season, while those that delay may avoid reproducing under suboptimal conditions. This flexibility enhances lifetime reproductive success across variable environments, a common strategy among small mammals with high extrinsic mortality rates.

Maximum longevity for the cotton mouse has been estimated at approximately 15 months [am = approximately 15 months] under natural conditions, though captive individuals have been known to survive considerably longer than their wild counterparts at a temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C]. Importantly, this lifespan estimate is derived from studies conducted at a standard body temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C], the typical core temperature for active, normothermic individuals. Few wild cotton mice survive beyond a single breeding season, as predation from owls, snakes, and carnivores imposes heavy mortality. The relatively short life expectancy has profound consequences for the species' life history, favoring early reproduction and high fecundity over extended somatic maintenance. Population turnover is rapid, and genetic diversity is maintained through high effective population sizes. Comparative data from related cricetid rodents suggest that this lifespan is near the upper limit for small-bodied species occupying high-risk habitats, underscoring the trade-off between longevity and reproductive output that defines the genus Peromyscus.
